analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers for every ton of carbon they sell and banks the revenue in a federal trust fund.
analysis.headline: A Democratic plan to charge fossil fuel producers for every ton of carbon they sell never got a hearing in either committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make coal producers, oil refiners, and other greenhouse gas producers and importers buy a federal permit for every ton of carbon dioxide their products would emit. The price of permits would be set by the Treasury Department on a five-year schedule so total emissions fall on a fixed path from 2011 through 2050. The money would go into a new Climate Protection and Economic Security Trust Fund meant to support clean energy and protect vulnerable families, and imports of carbon-intensive goods like steel and cement would face matching fees so foreign producers could not undercut U.S. companies. It never received a hearing or a vote in either committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary households would have gained from slower climate change and from trust fund spending aimed at protecting vulnerable families, and clean energy industries would have gained a predictable, rising carbon price that favors low-carbon technology. The bill's refunds for exporters and border fees on carbon-intensive imports were designed to shield steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, and chemical manufacturers from losing ground to foreign competitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households exposed to climate risks, clean energy firms

how_it_helps.text: It sets a firm national cap on greenhouse gas emissions that declines from about 6.8 billion tons of CO2-equivalent in 2011 to about 1.3 billion tons in 2050, forcing fossil fuel producers and refiners to buy a federal permit for every ton they sell.

Permit prices are set by the Treasury on a published five-year schedule rather than by trading, giving businesses and consumers a predictable, slowly rising carbon price instead of the volatility of a trading market.

It imposes a border fee on imports of carbon-intensive goods like steel, cement, aluminum, and glass equal to what U.S. producers pay in permits, and refunds permit costs to exporters, protecting domestic manufacturing jobs from unfair competition.
Revenue from permit sales goes into a Climate Protection and Economic Security Trust Fund intended to support clean energy and the economic security of vulnerable families and communities.

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers, oil refiners, and natural gas and other greenhouse gas producers and importers would pay permit fees on every ton they sell, and would pass those costs on to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, electricity, heating, and goods made with fossil energy. Energy-intensive manufacturers would face higher energy costs, though offset by refunds and import fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise the price of coal, oil, and natural gas, and fuel producers would pass permit costs to consumers in the form of higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices — costs that fall hardest on lower-income households.

By fixing prices administratively in five-year schedules rather than letting a market set them, the Secretary bears the risk of guessing wrong on demand, and the schedule can be changed only once (or twice in the first period) per five years, limiting flexibility if prices are set too low or too high.

The bill directs permit revenue into a Climate Protection and Economic Security Trust Fund but leaves the spending of that fund to future appropriation, so it guarantees no direct rebate to households facing higher energy prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The approach is a carbon tax-lite: fixed declining caps with government-set (not auctioned) prices, no trading, and border fees plus refunds to shield energy-intensive manufacturers — well designed on competitiveness and predictability. The main costs are higher fuel and electricity prices passed to households, and the bill's creation of a trust fund without specifying how revenue is returned to families leaves open the possibility that consumers bear the burden without visible offset. The emission cuts (roughly 80% by 2050) are deep and the price certainty is a genuine strength.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced; a Ways and Means subcommittee took jurisdiction the next day, but neither committee ever held a markup or vote, and the bill expired at the end of the 111th Congress.

narrative.text: H.R. 1683 was introduced by Rep. Jim McDermott on March 24, 2009 with seven cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The next day, March 25, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Environment.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas interests are better off, since no federal carbon charge was ever imposed on their products; households avoided the higher energy prices a carbon fee would have brought, but continued to bear the unpriced costs of carbon pollution.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel interests, which faced no carbon fee

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.role: Sponsor (D-WA), member of Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its carbon permit and trust fund provisions.

for.name: Reps. Blumenauer, Larson, and Stark
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Fossil fuel and carbon-intensive industries
against.role: Coal, oil, and manufacturing interests lobbying against carbon pricing
against.what_they_did: Opposed carbon-pricing legislation during the 111th Congress; the House-passed cap-and-trade bill (Waxman-Markey) ultimately stalled in the Senate.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after referring it to committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: They would have to buy a federal permit for every ton of carbon in the coal they sell, directly pricing their product out of part of the market as the cap tightens.

Refiners would pay permit fees on every barrel of crude and petroleum product received, raising costs that flow to consumers; the border fee and export refunds shield some of their downstream markets.

industries.industry: Natural gas and other greenhouse gas producers and importers
industries.note: Natural gas, methane, HFCs, and other greenhouse gases are covered substances subject to the same permit requirement.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: They would pay more for fuel, but the bill refunds permit costs on exported goods and charges equivalent fees on competing imports, largely insulating them from foreign competition.

A rising carbon price would make wind, solar, and efficiency more competitive against fossil fuels, expanding their market — but the bill channels the revenue into a generic trust fund rather than direct clean energy subsidies.
